abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Developed at Bayer Technology Services, PK‐Sim and MoBi transitioned into the Open Systems Pharmacology (OSP) Suite, released as free open‐source software in 2017. An active community with stakeholders from academia, industries, and regulators contributes to the continuous improvement of open‐source model‐informed drug development (MIDD). This perspective summarizes the latest advancements presented at the second OSP Community Conference (OSP‐CC) hosted from 29 to 30th of September 2025 at Sanofi Paris, that gathered over 100 attendees from more than 40 institutions.

sec.title: Conference Sessions & Covered Topics
sec.p: Conference sessions targeted applications and developments around the open‐source software [1], summarized in Table 1, on the Open Systems Pharmacology (https://www.open‐systems‐pharmacology.org/conference/), and GitHub resources (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology). For first time, additional satellite workshops were hosted, training the growing OSP community [2].

sec.title: Session 1: Clinical Applications/Development
Human Intestinal Organoids and Potential Application for PBPK Modeling
sec.p: Besides potential permeability and solubility limitations, active processes such as enzymatic metabolism and transporter activity may influence the observed bioavailability. Human intestinal organoids differentiated into functional epithelial monolayers were presented as an alternative to traditional Caco‐2 cell models. They express drug‐metabolizing enzymes like Cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 and Uridine Diphosphate Glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs), showing metabolic capabilities accounting for the intestinal first‐pass effect. A good correlation between contextualized PBPK models with organoid‐based in vitro measures and clinically observed bioavailability was found, confirming gut wall metabolism as a potential contributor to bioavailability limitations.

sec.title: Growing a Community‐Built Qualified OSP Suite Model Library
sec.p: A qualified OSP‐model library (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSP‐PBPK‐Model‐Library) is the basis for reproducible workflows. New OSP features and software releases, such as updating expression data, require a systematic reevaluation of the library (currently > 30 drug molecules and DDI interactions) and recreating model specific OSP‐Qualification‐Reports (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSP‐Qualification‐Reports). Updating ADME protein expression values with the latest RNAseq expression databases (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/Gene‐Expression‐Databases) requires parameter reidentification via OSPSuite.ParameterIdentification (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSPSuite.ParameterIdentification) as expression changes impact the pharmacokinetic profile [3]. An automated workflow updating model parameters was presented ensuring high model quality and continuous improvement of the OSP software.

sec.title: An Open Source In Silico Framework to Support Trial Design Decisions and Virtual Bioequivalence Assessments
sec.p: The presented OSP Virtual‐bioequivalence (VBE) toolbox (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/OSPSuite.VBE‐Toolbox) integrates in vitro and in vivo data, enabling the generation of probabilistic predictions of drug exposure across formulations [4]. These analyses can inform bioequivalence trials and serve as a potential alternative to traditional bioequivalence studies that compare a test formulation with an established reference product to streamline drug development reducing the reliance on costly clinical trials.

sec.title: Session 2: Clinical Applications/Development
Integrating Age‐ and BMI‐Related Changes to Form a Comprehensive Repository for Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic (PBPK) Modeling of Older People and People With Obesity
sec.p: Underrepresentation of older adults and adults with obesity in clinical trials can be a challenge for drug efficacy and safety assessment. A comprehensive database integrating age‐ and body mass index (BMI)‐related changes was presented, including updates of organ weights, blood flows, glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and CYP metabolism [5]. Validation was performed for renally‐cleared and CYP3A4‐metabolized compounds showing improvements for adults with obesity and age‐related pharmacokinetic changes.

sec.title: PBBM With OSP Suite: A Powerful Approach to Solving Bioequivalence Challenges in Regulated and Under Regulated Markets
sec.p: In Latin American markets, regulatory requirements for bioequivalence vary significantly, creating challenges for product evaluation, particularly in countries where similar drug products reach the market without bioequivalence studies [6]. Physiologically‐based biopharmaceutics modeling (PBBM) was used in case studies for carvedilol, furosemide, omeprazole to predict bioequivalence and product development in both regulated and under‐regulated markets. In the presented examples, sex differences in gastrointestinal physiology were highlighted as critical for accurate bioequivalence predictions.

sec.title: Bridging In Vitro Dissolution and In Vivo Pharmacokinetics: Application of a Novel Physiologically Based Biopharmaceutics Modeling (PBBM) Workflow to Vericiguat
sec.p: A PBBM workflow (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/Oral‐PBBM‐Workflow) was presented utilizing a solubility toolbox for characterizing pH‐ and bile salt‐effects on solubilization. An in vitro dissolution model with mechanistic particle dissolution equations for the US Pharmacopeia (USP) 2 dissolution apparatus and enhanced human PBPK capabilities with updated GI tract parameters were applied to vericiguat. The workflow successfully predicted fasted and fed‐state pharmacokinetics and drug–drug interactions (DDI) with omeprazole and demonstrates potential for biowaiver support, formulation optimization, and virtual bioequivalence studies [7].

sec.title: Session 3: Research & Discovery
Accelerating Drug Discovery: Systematic Application of PBPK Modeling Supporting Candidate Selection
sec.p: Applying PBPK models in early drug discovery requires fast model building and analysis based on a seamless integration of required model parameters. An OSP‐based high‐throughput PBPK platform was presented integrating measured compound information and machine learning models for parameter prediction to accelerate drug discovery. The system automates data transfer of 48 in vitro assays using decision trees selecting appropriate physicochemical and ADME parameters, while incorporated machine learning models predict missing property values. Validation across 575 rat and 150 monkey IV studies demonstrated good predictive performance for extended clearance classification system (ECCS) class 2 compounds, enabling systematic candidate assessment and supporting portfolio‐wide screening for complex disposition mechanisms.

sec.title: Prediction of Human Pharmacokinetics From Chemical Structure—Combining Mechanistic Modeling With Machine Learning
sec.p: Hybrid approaches combine machine learning with mechanistic modeling to predict pharmacokinetics directly from chemical structures. Combining graph convolutional neural networks (GNN) with PBPK models enabled prediction of key PK parameters (AUCiv, AUCpo, Cmax). Trained on ~10,000 compounds, a hybrid rat model was shown to achieve good exposure predictions after intravenous and oral administration [8]. The showcased approaches outperforms pure deep learning models and conventional scaling methods, particularly for oral exposure predictions, enabling early compound screening, prioritization, and dose predictions while reducing animal testing in accordance with 3R principles.

sec.title: Integrating In Vitro and In Silico Approaches Enables Accurate Prediction of Drug‐Induced Liver Injury
sec.p: Predicting drug‐induced toxicities as early as possible can help to focus on promising candidates and save valuable R&D resources. Combining in vitro toxicity assays with PBPK modeling was used to predict clinically known drug‐induced liver injury (DILI). Based on 241 drugs and in vitro toxicity assay data, clinical DILI outcomes were predicted using ratios of in vitro and PBPK model predicted Cmax values with good accuracy (ROC AUC 91%), outperforming simple heuristic screening rules (50%–70% accuracy). The presented approach demonstrates the potential of early DILI predictions aiming to reduce clinical failures and market withdrawals [9].

sec.title: Session 4: Submission, Lifecycle and Approval
Tools and Workflows for Automated Reporting of PBPK Modeling With OSP
sec.p: Manual preparation of reports and submission files is time consuming and error prone. An automated reporting workflow using ospsuite (https://www.open‐systems‐pharmacology.org/OSPSuite‐R/) and osp.snapshots (https://github.com/esqLABS/osp.snapshots) R packages was presented. By using standardized tables, text blocks, and figures, an automated model documentation and report generation process could be developed that significantly reduces reporting time while improving consistency and reducing manual errors in regulatory documentation generation.

sec.title: PBPK Modeling in Regulatory Submissions to the MHRA
sec.p: Acceptance of modeling analysis is key for successful applications. PBPK modeling can help to reduce clinical trial burden by predicting DDI, population‐specific effects, and absorption mechanisms informing dose selection. Model qualifications are critical, with requirements proportional to regulatory impact and patient risk requiring individual evaluation for each application. Successful case examples involving CYP3A4 inhibition, pediatric dosing, gastric pH effects, and nasal absorption were presented. Stricter scrutiny for high‐risk applications like extrapolations requires a robust qualification to support regulatory decisions.

sec.title: Software Verification, Validation, and Context of Use (CoU) Qualification of Open‐Source Modeling & Simulation Software for Regulatory Use in Translational MIDD
sec.p: The OSP platform uses GitHub for version control (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology), automated testing, and code quality analysis. The community addresses regulatory challenges through open‐source transparency and community‐driven qualification. A three‐pillar approach encompasses software validation, CoU qualification, and installation verification. A qualification framework allows automatic re‐qualification with new releases or data. Examples of MIDD applications accepted by regulatory agencies and an outlook expanding to modular PBPK‐QSP integration were presented.

sec.title: Session 5: Emerging Areas
Building a Qualifiable MIDD Ecosystem With Modular PBPK and QSP Models in OSP V12
sec.p: Modularization was introduced in OSP Suite V12 creating a qualifiable MIDD ecosystem with reusable components coping with a growing model complexity. Extension Modules reflecting organs, administration routes, disease states, or biomarkers can now be seamlessly combined with base PBPK models. Once developed, Extension Modules can be shared with the community via GitHub facilitating transparency, collaborative development, and reusability. The modularization concept is outlined in Figure 1.

caption.p: OSP Extension Module concept. PK‐Sim models are composed of individual Building Blocks (https://docs.open‐systems‐pharmacology.org/v12/open‐systems‐pharmacology‐suite/modules‐philsophy‐building‐blocks) separating information used for model building into dedicated groups. Building Blocks are combined to generate a model, they can be reused and combined to create different models. When transferring a PK‐SIM simulation to MoBi, model Building Blocks are further organized into a module. Modules represent either a full‐scale PBPK model imported from PK‐Sim (blue rectangle), or extension modules (orange rectangles) that represent model modifications or adaptations such as disease populations, custom administration routes, altered or new special structures that represent tissues or any other modification of the underlaying Building Blocks. Extension Modules provide a standardized, systematic, and reproducible way to efficiently develop and share complex models or model modifications across different projects and modeling scientists.

sec.title: PBPK‐PD Modeling of siRNAs
sec.p: An OSP model was presented addressing siRNA disposition, including liver‐targeted delivery and the formation of RNA‐induced silencing complex (RISC). Using a middle‐out approach validated across multiple siRNA compounds and species (mouse, monkey, human), the model successfully captures tissue distribution, target engagement, and pharmacological response [10]. However, key knowledge gaps in extravasation mechanisms, RISC dynamics, and species‐specific target variations still exist.

sec.title: Integrating Population Approaches With Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Models: A Novel Framework for Parameter Estimation
sec.p: The saemixPBPK (https://github.com/Sanofi‐Public/saemixPBPK) package was presented aiming to integrate population pharmacokinetic approaches in PBPK modeling. This hybrid approach combines the stochastic approximation expectation–maximization (SAEM) algorithm with mechanistic OSP models, enabling the estimation of individual parameters, quantification of interindividual variability, and assessment of covariate effects. The approach was evaluated using theophylline data with smoking status as a covariate and a drug–drug interaction study including itraconazole, resulting in more robust data‐informed predictions including population variability.

sec.title: Session 6: OSP Software Release Roadmap V13 and V14
sec.p: Current V12.1 delivers improvements such as parameter tracing, concurrent simulation execution, and batch chart editing (https://github.com/Open‐Systems‐Pharmacology/Suite/releases/). Software releases are forecasted as annual major and quarterly minor updates. V13 will focus on: (1) Standardized and automated qualification framework for MoBi projects, and (2) Extending the ospsuite (https://www.open‐systems‐pharmacology.org/OSPSuite‐R/) R package with MoBi functionalities. Anticipated features for V14 are (1) Incorporation of new populations for obesity and specific ethnicities, (2) additional absorption models, (3) extending the qualification framework, and (4) OSP support for Linux and MacOS. The community is encouraged to actively provide input and feedback shaping future development priorities.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The second OSP‐CC showcased recent advancements in PBPK modeling and their applications in MIDD, safety sciences, and QSP modeling. Highlights have been the integration of the latest automation and machine learning methods in various MIDD workflows. The OSP community is the driver behind these developments and features for mechanistic PBPK modeling that were presented over a wide range of topics. Here continuous collaboration, education, and coordination of activities among stakeholders drives further enhancements regarding functionality and usability. By showcasing successful applications of OSP across research & development, safety, and regulatory submissions, the community emphasizes the value of transparent and open‐source solutions that increase public trust, streamline innovation, and optimize resource allocation in MIDD and adjacent areas.
